Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

Let $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the Laurent polynomial ring and let
$\Lambda:=A[z]=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1},z]$ be the polynomial ring over $A$ in one
indeterminate ([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]],
[[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]). For $n\ge1$ let
$H(n):=\Lambda\otimes_AH_v(n)$ be the scalar extension of the generic type-A
Hecke algebra of [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]), so that $H(n)$ is the unital
$\Lambda$-algebra with generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ subject to
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v,\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1},\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(|i-j|>1),$$
and $H(1)=\Lambda$. The $\Lambda$-algebra $H(n)$ is free with basis
$\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$, where $T_w$ is the product of the generators along a reduced
word ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[def-symmetric-group]]).

The generators induce a $\Lambda$-algebra homomorphism
$\iota_n:H(n)\to H(n+1)$, $T_i\mapsto T_i$; it is injective, so we identify
$H(n)$ with its image, a $\Lambda$-subalgebra of $H(n+1)$.

A **Markov trace on the type-A Hecke tower** is a family of $\Lambda$-linear
maps $\operatorname{tr}_n:H(n)\to\Lambda$, $n\ge1$, such that

- (M1) $\operatorname{tr}_n(1)=1$ for one (equivalently, by (M2), every) $n$;
- (M2) $\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}\circ\iota_n=\operatorname{tr}_n$ for all $n\ge1$;
- (M3) $\operatorname{tr}_n(xy)=\operatorname{tr}_n(yx)$ for all $x,y\in H(n)$;
- (M4) $\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(x\,T_n)=z\,\operatorname{tr}_n(x)$ for all $n\ge1$
  and $x\in H(n)$.

Here $z\in\Lambda$ is a formal parameter, distinct from the Hecke parameter $v$;
no value of $z$ is fixed or inverted by this definition, and the trace takes
values in $\Lambda$, not in a field.

**Caveats.** This is a family over the whole tower, not a single functional; the
conditions (M1)--(M4) are a definition, so no trace is asserted to exist here
(existence and uniqueness is
[[thm-the-ocneanu-markov-trace-exists-and-is-unique]]). By (M3), (M4) is
equivalent to $\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(u\,T_n\,v)=z\operatorname{tr}_n(uv)$ for
all $u,v\in H(n)$: applied to $uT_nv$ one gets
$\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(uT_nv)=\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(T_nvu)=z\operatorname{tr}_n(vu)=z\operatorname{tr}_n(uv)$,
and conversely take $v=1$.

Let $H(1)\subset H(2)\subset\cdots$ be the type-A Hecke tower over
$\Lambda=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1},z]$ of [[def-markov-trace-on-the-type-a-hecke-tower]].
Then there exists a unique Markov trace $(\operatorname{tr}_n)_{n\ge1}$ on this
tower in the sense of [[def-markov-trace-on-the-type-a-hecke-tower]]. Moreover
it satisfies, for all $n\ge1$, all $x,y\in H(n)$ and all $1\le i\le n-1$:

- (a) $\operatorname{tr}_n(T_i)=z$;
- (b) $\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(xT_ny)=z\,\operatorname{tr}_n(xy)$;
- (c) $\operatorname{tr}_n$ is determined by (M1)--(M4) alone; it takes values in
  $\Lambda$ and is computed by iterating (b) along the free basis of
  [[lem-the-hecke-tower-is-free-over-the-previous-level]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\delta\in R$, and use the noncrossing-pairing diagram category of [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]], with the left factor stacked above the right factor. For a basis diagram $D:n\to n$, close each top endpoint to the corresponding bottom endpoint outside the rectangle and let $c(D)$ be the number of circles in the resulting finite graph. Define

$$\operatorname{Tr}_n(D)=\delta^{c(D)}$$

and extend $R$-linearly to $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$. This is the **unnormalized closure trace**. In particular, $\operatorname{Tr}_0(1_0)=1$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_n(1_n)=\delta^n$. No unit or nonzero condition on $\delta$ is required.

Let $\cup:0\to2$ and $\cap:2\to0$ be the standard cup and cap in the diagram category. For $n\ge1$ define the **right partial trace** by

$$\operatorname{ptr}_n(x)=(1_{n-1}\otimes\cap)\circ(x\otimes1_1)\circ(1_{n-1}\otimes\cup),\qquad x\in\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta).$$

It is a map $\mathrm{TL}_n\to\mathrm{TL}_{n-1}$. If $\delta$ is a unit, define $\tau_n=\delta^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}_n$. This agrees with the normalized trace of [[def-temperley-lieb-normalized-markov-trace-by-closure]] over $\mathbb C$ when $\delta\ne0$.

For any commutative ring $R$, loop value $\delta\in R$, and $n\ge0$, the unnormalized trace of [[def-temperley-lieb-closure-trace-and-partial-trace]] satisfies

$$\operatorname{Tr}_n(xy)=\operatorname{Tr}_n(yx),\qquad \operatorname{Tr}_{n+1}(x\otimes1)=\delta\operatorname{Tr}_n(x)$$

for $x,y\in\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$. For $n\ge1$ and $x\in\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$, it also satisfies

$$\operatorname{Tr}_{n+1}((x\otimes1)U_n)=\operatorname{Tr}_n(x),$$

where $U_n$ is the cup-cap generator on the last two strands of $\mathrm{TL}_{n+1}$. For $n\ge1$, $x\in\mathrm{TL}_{n-1}$ and $h\in\mathrm{TL}_n$,

$$\operatorname{Tr}_n\bigl(h(x\otimes1)\bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}_{n-1}\bigl(\operatorname{ptr}_n(h)x\bigr).$$

No division by $\delta$ occurs.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit and $\delta\in R$. For each $n\ge0$, let $F_n:=R\langle u_1,\ldots,u_{n-1}\rangle$ be the free associative unital $R$-algebra on the indicated symbols ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]). When $n=0$ or $n=1$, the symbol set is empty and $F_n=R$.

Let $I_n$ be the two-sided ideal generated by

$$u_i^2-\delta u_i\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad u_i u_j-u_j u_i\quad(|i-j|>1),$$

and

$$u_i u_{i+1}u_i-u_i,\qquad u_{i+1}u_i u_{i+1}-u_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2).$$

The abstract **rank-$n$ Temperley–Lieb algebra** is the presented $R$-algebra

$$P_n(R,\delta):=F_n/I_n.$$

Thus its defining relations are $u_i^2=\delta u_i$, $u_i u_{i\pm1}u_i=u_i$, and $u_i u_j=u_j u_i$ for $|i-j|>1$. The definition of a presented $R$-algebra and its universal property are those of [[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]].

For every $n\ge0$, each basis diagram in $\mathcal D(n,n)$ is a finite product of the elementary diagrams $d_1,\ldots,d_{n-1}$ from [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]]. The product can be chosen so that no intermediate stack creates a closed cycle. Therefore the set of diagrams lies in the unital subalgebra of $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ generated by these diagrams.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit, $\delta\in R$, and $n\ge0$. The homomorphism $\pi_n:P_n(R,\delta)\to\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ sending $u_i$ to $d_i$ is an isomorphism. Consequently the Jones normal forms of [[thm-temperley-lieb-generator-normal-form]] are an $R$-basis of the presented algebra, and both algebras are free of rank $C_n$. This holds without a field assumption and without requiring $\delta$ to be nonzero or invertible.

Let $H(1)\subset H(2)\subset\cdots$ be the Hecke tower of
[[def-markov-trace-on-the-type-a-hecke-tower]], with $H(n)$ free of rank $n!$
over $\Lambda$ with basis $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]), and for
$1\le i\le n$ put $w^{(i)}:=s_ns_{n-1}\cdots s_{n-i+1}$, $w^{(0)}:=1$. Then for
every $n\ge1$:

1. $H(n+1)$ is a free left $H(n)$-module with basis
   $T_{w^{(0)}},T_{w^{(1)}},\dots,T_{w^{(n)}}$: every element of $H(n+1)$ has a
   unique expression $\sum_{i=0}^{n}x_iT_{w^{(i)}}$ with $x_i\in H(n)$;
2. $H(n+1)$ is also a free right $H(n)$-module with basis
   $T_{(w^{(0)})^{-1}},T_{(w^{(1)})^{-1}},\dots,T_{(w^{(n)})^{-1}}$;
3. the  $H(n)$-sub-bimodule $H(n)T_nH(n)$ equals the direct sum
   $\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}H(n)T_{w^{(i)}}$, and the multiplication map
   $$H(n)\otimes_{H(n-1)}H(n)\longrightarrow H(n+1),\qquad x\otimes y\longmapsto xT_ny,$$
   is an isomorphism of $H(n)$-bimodules onto $H(n)T_nH(n)$; consequently
   $H(n+1)=H(n)\oplus H(n)T_nH(n)$ holds as a direct sum of $H(n)$-bimodules in
   the form $H(n+1)=H(n)\oplus\bigl(H(n)\otimes_{H(n-1)}H(n)\bigr)$. All three parts are proved here. Each chosen nonidentity minimal left-coset representative $w^{(i)}$
   has a displayed reduced expression containing $s_n$ exactly once; this does
   not characterize all basis elements whose reduced expressions contain
   $s_n$ once. In the tensor notation of part (3), set $H(0):=\Lambda$, the
   scalar extension $\Lambda\otimes_AH_v(0)$, so the $n=1$ case is defined.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Since $v+1=q^2+1=q\delta\ne0$, the assignment $T_i\mapsto qU_i-1$ is defined. Its quadratic relation follows from $(qU_i-1-v)(qU_i)=q^2(U_i-\delta)U_i=0$, using $v=q^2$ and $U_i^2=\delta U_i$. For adjacent generators, expanding both braid words gives difference $q^3(U_iU_{i+1}U_i-U_{i+1}U_iU_{i+1})-q^2\delta(U_i-U_{i+1})+q(U_i-U_{i+1})=0$, since $q^2\delta=q^3+q$. Distant commutation is inherited, so the assignment defines a tower homomorphism; it is surjective by [F4].

Put $E_i=\sum_{w\in\langle s_i,s_{i+1}\rangle}T_w$, the six-term expression in the Statement. Expanding with the Hecke quadratic and braid relations gives $(T_i+1)(T_{i+1}+1)(T_i+1)=E_i+v(T_i+1)$. Under $T_j+1=qU_j$, the left side maps to $q^3U_iU_{i+1}U_i=q^3U_i$ and the second term maps to $q^3U_i$, so $\phi_n(E_i)=0$. Since $J_n$ is the two-sided ideal generated by the $E_i$, $\phi_n(J_n)=0$ and $\phi_n$ factors through $H(n)/J_n$.

The pullback $\widetilde\tau_n:=\tau_n\circ\phi_n$ is cyclic and has $\widetilde\tau_n(1)=1$ by [F3]. For $n\ge1$ and $x\in H(n)$, its image in $\mathrm{TL}_{n+1}$ is $\phi_n(x)\otimes1$, and $T_n$ maps to $qU_n-1$, so $\widetilde\tau_{n+1}(xT_n)=(q/\delta-1)\tau_n(\phi_n(x))=-\widetilde\tau_n(x)/(q\delta)=-\widetilde\tau_n(x)/(q^2+1)=z_0\widetilde\tau_n(x)$. The tower restriction rule follows from [F3]; hence $\widetilde\tau$ satisfies the specialized Markov rules.

The presentation [F4] gives $\psi_n:\mathrm{TL}_n\to H(n)/J_n$ by $U_i\mapsto q^{-1}(T_i+1)$. The Hecke quadratic relation gives $U_i^2=\delta U_i$ for these images, while step 2.1 in the quotient gives $(T_i+1)(T_{i+1}+1)(T_i+1)=q^2(T_i+1)$ and hence $U_iU_{i+1}U_i=U_i$; the other adjacent relation follows by interchanging indices and distant commutation is inherited. Thus $\psi_n$ is well defined. Its composites with the map induced by $\phi_n$ fix each generator: $U_i\mapsto q^{-1}(qU_i-1+1)=U_i$ and $T_i\mapsto q(q^{-1}(T_i+1))-1=T_i$. Therefore $H(n)/J_n\cong\mathrm{TL}_n$, proving the quotient isomorphism.

The decomposition in [F5] writes every element of $H(n+1)$ as a sum of an element of $H(n)$ and terms $xT_ny$ with $x,y\in H(n)$. For any Markov trace, restriction determines the first term; cyclicity and (M4) force $\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(xT_ny)=z\operatorname{tr}_n(xy)$ on each remaining term. Induction from $H(1)=\mathbb C$ therefore shows at most one specialized trace can satisfy (M1)--(M4), even when $v,z$ have been specialized: this uses only the free decomposition [F5], not division by a parameter. By step 2.2 the pullback $\widetilde\tau$ is such a trace, so it is the specialized Ocneanu trace. Since $\phi_n(J_n)=0$, the trace vanishes on all of the two-sided ideal $J_n$. The quotient isomorphism of step 3.1 identifies the descended functional with the normalized closure trace $\tau_n$.

boundaries.reason: The Hecke tower proof is based at H(1)=C in step 4.1. The closure convention nevertheless retains Tr0(1_0)=1 and rank-zero unit/tower identities; it does not introduce T0 or U0.

F3 keeps unit and tower trace identities for n>=0 and the U_n rule only for n>=1; step 2.2 explicitly uses n>=1. The allowed lower root ell3 has delta1 and no undefined U0.

Let $(V,B)$ be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate real quadratic space with $Q(v)=B(v,v)$, and let $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ use $v^2=Q(v)1$. Use the grading involution $\alpha$ and Clifford conjugation $\bar x$ from [[lem-real-clifford-involutions-and-norm]]. Let $\mathrm{Cl}^0$ and $\mathrm{Cl}^1$ be the even and odd parts for word-length parity. Define the **unrestricted twisted Clifford normalizer** as the set

$$\Gamma(V,B)=\{x\in\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)^\times:\alpha(x)v x^{-1}\in V\text{ for every }v\in V\},\qquad \rho_x(v)=\alpha(x)v x^{-1}.$$

Define the normalized anisotropic vectors $U(V,Q)=\{u\in V:|Q(u)|=1\}$. For $\dim V>0$, **Pin$(V,Q)$** is the subgroup of $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)^\times$ generated by $U(V,Q)$; for $V=0$, set Pin$(0)=\{1,-1\}$. Define

$$\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(V,Q)=\operatorname{Pin}(V,Q)\cap\mathrm{Cl}^0,\qquad \operatorname{Spin}_{N=1}(V,Q)=\{x\in\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(V,Q):N(x)=1\}.$$

For definite signature, the conventional names Pin$^+(n)$ and Pin$^-(n)$ mean the groups in $\mathrm{Cl}_{n,0}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,n}$, respectively. In mixed signature the subscript “full” is retained because the full even subgroup and the norm-one subgroup can have different images.

Let $\Gamma$, Pin, $\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}$, $N(x)=x\bar x$, and $\rho$ have the definitions in [[def-real-clifford-group-and-normalized-pin-spin]] and [[lem-real-clifford-involutions-and-norm]]. Then $N$ is scalar-valued and multiplicative on $\Gamma$. For $x=u_1\cdots u_k$ with anisotropic $u_j$,

$$N(x)=\prod_{j=1}^k(-Q(u_j)).$$

The subgroup generated by $|Q(u)|=1$ vectors is exactly $\{x\in\Gamma:N(x)\in\{1,-1\}\}$; it consists of normalized anisotropic-vector products, with scalar $-1$ included when $V=0$. Its even part consists of the even products and is $\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}$; $\operatorname{Spin}_{N=1}$ is the norm-one subgroup of this full even group.

Let $(V,B)$ be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate real quadratic space, $Q(v)=B(v,v)$, and let $\Gamma$ and $\rho_x(v)=\alpha(x)vx^{-1}$ be as in [[def-real-clifford-group-and-normalized-pin-spin]]. For anisotropic $u$, $\rho_u=r_u$. Every $x\in\Gamma$ acts by an element of $O(V,B)$, is homogeneous, and is a nonzero scalar times a product of anisotropic vectors. The kernel of $x\mapsto\rho_x$ on $\Gamma$ is exactly $\mathbb R^\times 1$; consequently the unrestricted normalizer in the definition is a group and agrees with its homogeneous part.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic not $2$, let $V$ be finite-dimensional of dimension $n$, and let $B$ be any symmetric bilinear form on $V$, possibly degenerate; put $Q(v)=B(v,v)$. Fix an ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$. Then

$$1,\qquad \bar e_{i_1}\cdots\bar e_{i_r}\quad(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_r\le n)$$

is a $k$-basis of $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$, so $\dim_k\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)=2^n$. Give $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ the word-length filtration $F_{-1}=0$ and, for $m\ge0$, let $F_m$ be the span of products of at most $m$ canonical generators. The natural graded algebra map

$$\Lambda V\longrightarrow\operatorname{gr}_F\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}F_m/F_{m-1}$$

that sends $v\in V$ to the degree-one class of $\bar v$ is an isomorphism, where the graded product is induced by $F_pF_q\subseteq F_{p+q}$. No nondegeneracy hypothesis is needed.

Let $k,V,B,Q$ be as in [[def-clifford-algebra-of-a-quadratic-space]], and let $A$ be a unital associative $k$-algebra. For every $k$-linear map $f:V\to A$ satisfying $f(v)^2=Q(v)1_A$ for all $v\in V$, there is a unique unital $k$-algebra homomorphism $\bar f:\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)\to A$ such that $\bar f\circ i_Q=f$.

derivations.claim: In $\mathrm{Cl}_{1,0}$, $e^2=1$ and the unit-vector-generated Pin group is $\{1,-1,e,-e\}$; its reflection lift $e$ has square $+1$. In $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,1}$, $f^2=-1$ and Pin is $\{1,-1,f,-f\}\cong C_4$; its reflection lift has square $-1$. In both cases the even subgroup is $\{1,-1\}$.

In $\mathrm{Cl}_{2,0}$ put $E=e_1e_2$. Then $E^2=-1$, and by [F3] the even algebra is exactly $\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb R E\cong\mathbb C$. For $a^2+b^2=1$, $a+bE$ is a product of two unit vectors: $e_1(ae_1+be_2)=a+bE$. Thus every unit $a+bE$ belongs to Spin, and conversely every even unit product has norm one, so Spin$(2)=\{a+bE:a^2+b^2=1\}$.

The matrices in the Example satisfy $A^2=B^2=I$ and $AB=-BA=\operatorname{diag}(-i,i)$. Hence $(z_1A+z_2B)^2=(z_1^2+z_2^2)I$ for all $z_1,z_2\in\mathbb C$. Applying [F4] to the complexification of the positive plane defines a unital complex Clifford action on $S$. Its image contains $P_+=(I+iAB)/2=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and $P_-=(I-iAB)/2=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$, as well as $P_+A$ and $P_-A$, which are the other two matrix units. The image is therefore all of $M_2(\mathbb C)$; [F3] gives complex dimension $4$ for the source, so this map is an algebra isomorphism. Every nonzero invariant subspace contains both coordinate vectors by applying these matrix units to a nonzero vector, proving irreducibility of the complex dimension-$2$ Clifford module.

For $\theta\in\mathbb R$, let $g_\theta=\cos(\theta/2)-E\sin(\theta/2)$. Since $g_\theta^{-1}=\cos(\theta/2)+E\sin(\theta/2)$, direct multiplication using $Ee_1=-e_2$ and $e_1E=e_2$ gives $\rho_{g_\theta}(e_1)=\cos\theta\,e_1+\sin\theta\,e_2$ and $\rho_{g_\theta}(e_2)=-\sin\theta\,e_1+\cos\theta\,e_2$. Therefore the angle doubles; $g_{2\pi}=-1$ and $g_{4\pi}=1$.

Since $c(E)=AB=\operatorname{diag}(-i,i)$, the operator $c(\omega)=iAB$ has the displayed eigenspaces $S^\pm$, each a complex line. Restricting the Clifford action to the circle in step 1.2 gives on these lines the scalars $a-ib$ and $a+ib$, of absolute value one. The scalar functions are continuous in $(a,b)$, and multiplicativity of the Clifford action makes them group characters; the one-dimensional modules are irreducible. They are inequivalent because the Spin element $E$ acts by $-i$ on $S^+$ and $i$ on $S^-$. Substituting $a=\cos(\theta/2)$ and $b=-\sin(\theta/2)$ yields the two asserted half-angle actions. In particular the kernel element $g_{2\pi}=-1$ acts by $-1$ and $g_{4\pi}=1$ acts by $1$, consistently with the vector double-angle map in step 2.1.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

Let $H,K$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, let $\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be a quantum channel ([[def-qc-quantum-channel]]), and let $A,B$ be non-negative operators on $H$. Then

$$D(\Phi(A)\|\Phi(B))\le D(A\|B).$$

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $(E_y)_{y\in\Omega}$ be a finite POVM on $H$, where $\Omega=\{y_0,\ldots,y_{m-1}\}$ is a fixed enumeration of its nonempty outcome set. Let $K=\mathbb C^m$ with standard orthonormal basis $(f_0,\ldots,f_{m-1})$, and set $\Pi_jz:=\langle z,f_j\rangle f_j$, the rank-one projection onto $f_j$ under the root linear-first convention. The map $\mathcal M_E(X):=\sum_{j<m}\operatorname{tr}(XE_{y_j})\Pi_j$ is a quantum channel from $H$ to $K$. For the indexed register $\mathbb C^\Omega$ with orthonormal basis $|y\rangle$, the unitary identification $Jf_j=|y_j\rangle$ gives the equivalent channel $X\mapsto\sum_{y\in\Omega}\operatorname{tr}(E_yX)|y\rangle\langle y|=J\mathcal M_E(X)J^*$. Thus either finite outcome-register convention is covered.

For probability vectors $p=(p_i)_{i\in I}$ and $q=(q_i)_{i\in I}$ on a finite nonempty set $I$, define

$$D(p\|q):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln\frac{p_i}{q_i},&p_i>0\Rightarrow q_i>0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Then $D(p\|q)\ge0$, and $D(p\|q)=0$ if and only if $p=q$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

Let $\rho$ be a density operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$, and let $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ be a finite POVM on $H$. Then

$$p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)\in[0,1]\quad\text{for each }a\in\Omega,\qquad \sum_{a\in\Omega}p_\rho(a)=1.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $A,B:H\to H$ be non-negative operators. For such an operator $A$, set $\operatorname{supp}(A):=(\ker A)^\perp$, where $\ker A$ is the kernel of a linear map ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]); this extends the density-operator support convention in [[def-qc-density-operator]]. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, define

$$D(A\|B):=\operatorname{tr}(A\ln A)-\operatorname{tr}(A\ln B).$$

Here $\ln A$ is defined spectrally on the positive eigenspaces of $A$ with $0\ln0:=0$, and $\ln B$ in the cross term is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}(B)$; the support condition ensures that $A$ vanishes on $\ker B$, so the omitted kernel contributes zero. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\nsubseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, set $D(A\|B):=+\infty$. In particular, $D(0\|B)=0$. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional **quantum relative entropy**. The logarithms are natural, so the value is in nats; the base-two value is $D_2(A\|B):=D(A\|B)/\ln2$.

derivations.claim: The singleton POVM $E_0=I_H$ is a finite POVM by [F4]. By [F8] the inputs have trace one, and [F2] sends each density operator to the scalar state $1$ on a one-dimensional register. Applying [F1] gives $D(\rho\|\sigma)\ge D(1\|1)=0$ by [F10].

Suppose $D(\rho\|\sigma)=0$ and choose any orthonormal basis $(e_j)_{j<d}$ of $H$ using [F7]. The rank-one maps $P_jx:=\langle x,e_j\rangle e_j$ are self-adjoint and satisfy $\langle P_jx,x\rangle=|\langle x,e_j\rangle|^2\ge0$ by [F9], so they are non-negative by [F6]. Their sum is $I_H$, so [F4] makes them a finite POVM; it has nonempty outcome set because $H\ne\{0\}$. By [F5], the outcome vectors $p_j=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_j)$ and $q_j=\operatorname{tr}(\sigma P_j)$ are probability vectors. Data processing [F1] and classical KL nonnegativity [F3] give $0=D(\rho\|\sigma)\ge D(p\|q)\ge0$, so $p_j=q_j$ for every $j$.

For any unit vector $v\in H$, extend $v$ to an orthonormal basis using [F7]. Step 1.2 applied to that basis gives $\langle\rho v,v\rangle=\langle\sigma v,v\rangle$; by homogeneity this equality holds for every $v$. Put $\Delta=\rho-\sigma$, which is self-adjoint by [F6], and $q(v)=\langle\Delta v,v\rangle$. Under the root convention [F9], expansion gives $4\langle\Delta x,y\rangle=q(x+y)-q(x-y)+i q(x+iy)-i q(x-iy)$. Since every $q(v)=0$, all matrix coefficients of $\Delta$ vanish, hence $\rho=\sigma$.
Conversely, if $\rho=\sigma$, [F10] gives the support inclusion, and the two spectral logarithmic traces in the QRE definition agree, so $D(\rho\|\sigma)=0$.
